Female Big brown bats typically achieve an ultimate adult body mass of approximately 25 grams [Wwi = approximately 25 grams] at maturity, whereas conspecific males tend to reach a somewhat lower asymptotic value of about 20 grams [Wwi = about 20 grams]. This degree of sexual size dimorphism, with females averaging roughly 23 grams across populations, is a common pattern among temperate insectivorous vespertilionids and is often attributed to the energetic demands of gestation and lactation. Neonates emerge weighing a modest 3.9 grams [Wwb = 3.9 grams] at birth, a value consistent with the altricial developmental strategy typical of the family. At a regulated body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], gestation proceeds for a period of 35 days [tg = 35 days], a duration that aligns closely with predictions based on maternal mass for mammals of this size. Following parturition, the dependent pups enter a suckling phase characterized by rapid mass gain. Nutritional independence is attained at weaning, when the young reach a wet weight of 17.2 grams [Wwx = 17.2 grams], representing an approximately 4.4-fold increase in mass relative to their birth weight.

Reproductive output in Eptesicus fuscus is constrained by the species' temperate latitude and prolonged hibernation period. Females give birth to a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], typically consisting of two pups per litter [N_R_i = two pups per litter]. This annual reproductive output, consisting of one litter per year with two pups each, is modest compared to many small mammals but is characteristic of bats, which exhibit among the lowest fecundity rates for their body size among eutherians. The observed litter size appears to be optimized for the species' relatively long lifespan and slow life-history pace. Field studies indicate that juvenile survival is high, and the production of a single annual litter likely reflects a trade-off between current reproductive investment and future survival. At 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of one litter per year with two pups represents an upper bound that is rarely realized under natural conditions. This figure integrates both the constraints imposed by the 35-day gestation and the lengthy period of post-natal care.

The timing of key life-history transitions in Eptesicus fuscus is tightly regulated by the species' thermoregulatory physiology. Under a sustained body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], female bats reach sexual maturity at 547 days after birth [tp = 547 days after birth], a delay of approximately one and a half years that reflects the extended juvenile growth phase characteristic of temperate bats. Males, by contrast, attain puberty later, at 730 days after birth [tp = 730 days after birth], a two-year interval that likely reflects the additional time required to develop the body condition necessary for successful competition for mating opportunities at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This sex-specific difference in maturation timing is well documented among vespertilionids and is thought to be driven by the higher energetic costs associated with male reproductive behaviors such as territorial defense and scent-marking. The relatively late onset of reproductive maturity in both sexes, particularly in males, is a key life-history trait that underpins the species' low intrinsic rate of increase.

Maximum longevity in the Big brown bat has been estimated at approximately 19 years [am = approximately 19 years] under field conditions when measured at a reference body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. This exceptionally long lifespan for a mammal of only 20 to 25 grams adult body mass places Eptesicus fuscus among the most long-lived species relative to body size, a characteristic shared with many chiropterans. The species' extended longevity is thought to be linked to its ability to enter daily torpor and seasonal hibernation, metabolic strategies that reduce oxidative damage and slow the accumulation of cellular wear. The approximately 19-year estimate is derived from mark-recapture studies of wild populations and represents the maximum recorded interval between initial capture and final sighting. Captive individuals may survive for comparable durations when provided with adequate nutrition and veterinary care. This remarkable lifespan is a central feature of the species' slow life-history strategy, enabling it to sustain low annual fecundity rates while maintaining stable population sizes.

Comparative analyses of body mass dynamics reveal that the ontogenetic trajectory of Eptesicus fuscus reflects a strategy common among small, temperate vespertilionids: rapid pre-weaning mass gain followed by a prolonged period of gradual somatic growth. The mass at birth, at approximately 3.9 grams, represents only about 16 percent of the adult female asymptotic mass of 25 grams, underscoring the altricial condition of the neonate. Pups more than quadruple their birth mass over the nursing period, reaching a weaning mass of 17.2 grams before transitioning to independent foraging. After weaning, juvenile growth slows considerably, and the asymptotic adult body masses of approximately 25 grams in females and 20 grams in males are not attained until after the first year of life. This pattern of early accelerated growth followed by a protracted approach to adult size is consistent with the energetic constraints imposed by hibernation and the seasonal availability of insect prey in temperate environments. Sex-specific differences in ultimate adult mass are modest but consistent across studied populations, with females maintaining a slight size advantage that likely confers reproductive benefits during gestation and lactation.
